idea.en: Tilt posterior from the four chamber to open the coronary sinus.

alt.en: Echo Lab render of the Apical coronary sinus view. Tilt posterior in small steps until the venous tube appears.

caption.en: Echo Lab render of the Apical coronary sinus view. Tilt posterior in small steps until the venous tube appears.

steps.en: What you see: A dark tube runs in the posterior groove and drains into the right atrium beside the tricuspid valve. It stays thin in health and widens when right atrial pressure rises or a left sided vena cava persists.
Landmarks to confirm: Do not accept the view until each of these is on screen.
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Each mistake below comes from the view catalogue with its correction.
Normal values: A dilated sinus with a 21 mm cava and poor collapse points to right atrial pressure near 15 mmHg.
Right atrial pressure reads near 3 mmHg when the cava is 21 mm or less with collapse above 50 percent.
Report sinus diameter in millimetres and note the phase used, since no named guideline defines a standard timing.

Pitfalls: Agitated saline from the left arm opacifies a persistent left vena cava through the sinus before the right atrium; from the right arm the atrium lights first. Do not confuse Thebesian valve tissue at the mouth with thrombus.

spot.en: Common mistakes and how to correct them: Mistaking the coronary sinus for the descending aorta. Correct it by checking pulsation and direction, since the aorta pulses and runs away from the atrium.
Losing the sinus by tilting too far posterior. Correct it by tilting back anterior until the atrium returns and then advancing in small steps.
Confusing posterior pericardial fluid with the vessel lumen. Correct it by looking for walls and venous flow, since fluid has neither.

todo.en: How to get it: Place the probe at apex, fifth intercostal space, tilted posterior from four chamber.
Point the probe marker toward the left, about three o clock.
From the four chamber, tilt the tail posterior slowly until the tube appears in the groove. Colour helps: steady venous flow fills it, while the aorta pulses.
Freeze the image only when every listed landmark is on screen at once.

remember.en: Use a dilated sinus as a clue to venous anomalies.

q.en: How do you separate coronary sinus from descending aorta?

o.en: By pulsation and flow direction with colour

why.en: The aorta pulses and runs away from the atrium while the sinus shows venous flow.

q.en: Saline from the left arm lights the sinus before the atrium. What does this mean?

why.en: Early sinus opacification from the left arm marks a persistent left vena cava.

q.en: Posterior echo free space has no walls and no flow. What is it?

why.en: Fluid without walls or flow is pericardial fluid, not a vessel.

sources: ASE 2019 guideline for the complete transthoracic examination, modified apical views section.
ASE 2010 right heart guideline, inferior vena cava section.
objectives: Tilt posterior from the four chamber to open the coronary sinus.
Tell the sinus from the descending aorta and from fluid.
Use a dilated sinus as a clue to venous anomalies.
